crafts.name: Bishnupur Terracotta Craft
crafts.description: One of the most celebrated traditional clay crafts of West Bengal, associated with the terracotta temples built under the Malla kings in the 17th and 18th centuries. Stone being scarce in the region, artisans used locally available clay to create detailed architectural panels depicting scenes from Hindu mythology, epics such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata, royal life, social activities, animals and floral motifs. Over generations the artisans of Bishnupur have carried the tradition into decorative sculptures, religious figures and artistic objects, narrating historical and social stories through terracotta.

crafts.name: Jaipur Blue Pottery
crafts.description: A distinctive craft of Rajasthan known for blue and turquoise designs under a glossy glazed finish. Unlike conventional pottery it does not primarily use clay, resting instead on a quartz-based technique. Its origins are Persian and Central Asian, reaching India through cultural exchange during the Mughal period, and it was later promoted under the royal patronage of Jaipur's rulers with revival efforts through the 19th and 20th centuries. Artisans produce decorative and functional objects carrying floral, geometric and nature-inspired motifs.

crafts.name: Nizamabad Black Pottery
crafts.description: A traditional pottery form from Nizamabad town in Azamgarh district, distinguished by its black surface and intricate silver-like engraved patterns, which set it apart from other pottery traditions of India. The tradition is believed to have developed several centuries ago among local artisan communities and has passed down through generations. It holds a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in recognition of its artistic value.

crafts.name: Kutch Lippan Mud-and-Mirror Work
crafts.description: A traditional mud-relief and mirror decoration craft practised by artisan communities of the Kutch region. 'Lippan' refers to the process of applying mud or clay to surfaces for decorative purposes; traditionally it ornamented the interiors of Bhunga houses, the circular traditional homes of Kutch, where the designs carried both aesthetic beauty and cultural identity. Geometric patterns, floral motifs and embedded mirrors express the region's visual language, and artisans have since adapted the work from architectural decoration into contemporary home decor while preserving its traditional essence.

crafts.name: Ghurni Clay Doll Craft
crafts.description: One of India's most renowned traditional clay modelling traditions, known worldwide for exceptional realism, detailed expressions and lifelike representation of human figures, animals and social characters. Associated with the patronage of Maharaja Krishna Chandra during the 18th century, artisans created realistic miniature representations of rural life, occupations and cultural events. Its uniqueness lies in the attention given to facial expression, body posture, costume and minute detail, making it an important example of Bengal's sculptural heritage.
